```{=html}

⚡ Building Interactive Apps with Shiny

A practical lecture note for analysts ready to move beyond static reports

``` If you've ever finished an R analysis and thought *"I wish my manager could just drag a slider and see this update"* — that's exactly what **Shiny** solves. Shiny is an R package developed by Posit (formerly RStudio) that lets you turn ordinary R code into a fully interactive web application — without writing a single line of JavaScript, HTML, or CSS (unless you want to). Your colleague can open a URL in a browser, adjust inputs, and see outputs update in real time, all powered by R running on a server behind the scenes. ::: {.callout-note} ## The core idea in one sentence Shiny wraps R in a reactive framework: when an **input** changes (a slider, a dropdown, a text box), any **output** that depends on it automatically re-runs and updates. ::: --- ## The Two-Part Structure Every Shiny app has exactly two logical pieces: | Part | What it does | Where it lives | |---|---|---| | **UI** (`ui`) | Defines the layout and controls the user sees | `ui.R` or the `ui` object | | **Server** (`server`) | Contains the R code that produces outputs | `server.R` or the `server` function | You can write these in two separate files (`ui.R` + `server.R`) or in a single `app.R` file. For learning purposes, a single file is easiest. --- ## Your First Shiny App (10 Lines) Here is the smallest working Shiny app. It takes a number from a slider and shows its square root. ```{r} library(shiny) ui <- fluidPage( sliderInput("n", "Pick a number", min = 1, max = 100, value = 25), textOutput("result") ) server <- function(input, output) { output$result <- renderText({ paste("Square root of", input$n, "is", round(sqrt(input$n), 3)) }) } shinyApp(ui, server) ``` ::: {.callout-tip} ## Try it yourself Paste this into RStudio and click **Run App**. You'll see a slider and a line of text. Drag the slider — notice the text updates instantly. That instant update is Shiny's reactive system doing its job. ::: --- ## Understanding Reactivity Reactivity is what makes Shiny feel alive. The rule is simple: > **Any output that reads `input$x` will automatically re-run whenever `input$x` changes.** You don't call a refresh function. You don't write event listeners. Shiny tracks the dependency for you. ### The reactive graph ``` [sliderInput: n] ──────► [renderText: result] ``` If you had two outputs both reading `input$n`, they would both re-run when the slider moves. If you had an output that reads `input$a` and `input$b`, it re-runs when *either* changes. ### `reactive()` — sharing computed values If multiple outputs need the same intermediate computation, don't repeat the code. Wrap it in `reactive()`: ```{r} server <- function(input, output) { # Computed once, shared by multiple outputs filtered_data <- reactive({ mtcars[mtcars$cyl == input$cyl, ] }) output$plot <- renderPlot({ plot(filtered_data()$wt, filtered_data()$mpg) }) output$table <- renderTable({ filtered_data() }) } ``` Note: you call a reactive expression like a function — `filtered_data()` — with parentheses. --- ## Key UI Components Shiny has built-in input and output widgets for almost everything you need. ### Inputs ```{r} # Numeric input sliderInput("year", "Select year:", min = 2018, max = 2024, value = 2022) # Dropdown selectInput("channel", "Channel:", choices = c("Mobile", "Paid Search", "Affiliate", "Social Media")) # Checkbox group checkboxGroupInput("methods", "Attribution methods:", choices = c("First Touch", "Last Touch", "Markov"), selected = "Markov") # Date range dateRangeInput("dates", "Date range:", start = "2024-01-01", end = Sys.Date()) ``` ### Outputs ```{r} # In the UI: declare where each output goes plotOutput("my_chart") tableOutput("my_table") textOutput("my_text") verbatimTextOutput("my_code_output") # In the server: produce each output output$my_chart <- renderPlot({ ... }) output$my_table <- renderTable({ ... }) output$my_text <- renderText({ ... }) ``` --- ## A More Realistic Example: Attribution Explorer Here is a Shiny app closer to something you might actually use — an interactive attribution comparison tool: ```{r} library(shiny) library(ggplot2) library(dplyr) # Data attr_data <- data.frame( channel = rep(c("Mobile", "Paid Search", "Affiliate", "Social Media"), 3), method = rep(c("First Touch", "Last Touch", "Markov"), each = 4), credits = c(21, 34, 17, 10, # first touch 26, 15, 18, 8, # last touch 21, 20, 20, 21) # markov ) ui <- fluidPage( titlePanel("Attribution Model Explorer"), sidebarLayout( sidebarPanel( checkboxGroupInput( "methods", "Select attribution models:", choices = unique(attr_data$method), selected = unique(attr_data$method) ), hr(), p("Adjust which models to display and compare how each model assigns credit to the four marketing channels.") ), mainPanel( plotOutput("attr_chart", height = "400px"), hr(), tableOutput("attr_table") ) ) ) server <- function(input, output) { filtered <- reactive({ attr_data |> filter(method %in% input$methods) }) output$attr_chart <- renderPlot({ ggplot(filtered(), aes(x = channel, y = credits, fill = method)) + geom_col(position = "dodge", width = 0.65) + scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") + labs(title = "Conversion Credits by Channel and Model", x = NULL, y = "Credits", fill = "Model") + theme_minimal(base_size = 14) }) output$attr_table <- renderTable({ filtered() |> tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = method, values_from = credits) }) } shinyApp(ui, server) ``` --- ## Layout Options Shiny gives you several layout options to structure more complex apps. ### `sidebarLayout()` — most common Controls on the left, output on the right. Used in the example above. ### `navbarPage()` — multi-tab apps ```{r} ui <- navbarPage( "My App", tabPanel("Overview", plotOutput("overview_plot")), tabPanel("Data Table", tableOutput("data_table")), tabPanel("About", p("This app was built with Shiny.")) ) ``` ### `fluidRow()` + `column()` — custom grids ```{r} ui <- fluidPage( fluidRow( column(4, wellPanel(sliderInput(...))), column(8, plotOutput("chart")) ) ) ``` --- ## How to Deploy a Shiny App A Shiny app requires a **live R process** to run. That means you can't just put the files on a web server like a static HTML page — you need somewhere R is actually executing. | Option | Cost | Difficulty | Best for | |---|---|---|---| | **shinyapps.io** (Posit) | Free tier available | Easy | Sharing with anyone | | **Posit Connect** | Paid (org license) | Medium | Internal enterprise use | | **Shiny Server** (self-hosted) | Free (server cost) | Hard | Full control | | **Docker + cloud** | Pay-as-you-go | Hard | Production scale | For class and portfolio purposes, **shinyapps.io** is the easiest path: ```{r} # Install rsconnect and deploy install.packages("rsconnect") library(rsconnect) # Authenticate once (get token from shinyapps.io) rsconnect::setAccountInfo(name = "YOUR_ACCOUNT", token = "YOUR_TOKEN", secret = "YOUR_SECRET") # Deploy rsconnect::deployApp(appDir = "path/to/your/app/") ``` --- ## Common Mistakes (and How to Fix Them) ::: {.callout-warning} ### Mistake 1: Forgetting parentheses on reactive expressions `filtered_data` is a function — you must call it as `filtered_data()`. ::: ::: {.callout-warning} ### Mistake 2: Putting heavy computation outside `reactive()` Code at the top level of `server` runs *once* at startup. If you need something to re-run when inputs change, it must be inside `reactive()`, `renderPlot()`, etc. ::: ::: {.callout-warning} ### Mistake 3: Using `input$x` outside a reactive context You can only read input values inside `reactive()`, `render*()`, or `observe()`. Reading `input$x` directly in a regular function will throw an error. ::: --- ## Summary Shiny lets you go from an R script to a shareable, interactive web app without leaving R. The mental model is: 1. **UI** describes what the user sees and interacts with. 2. **Server** contains the R logic that produces outputs. 3. **Reactivity** connects them automatically — change an input, outputs update. For analysts already comfortable in R and ggplot2, Shiny is a natural next step. The learning curve is mostly about understanding reactivity, not about R itself. ::: {.callout-note} ## What comes next? In the next essay, we look at **Shinylive** — a way to run Shiny apps entirely in the browser, with no server required. :::
